children: Michael Burry is questioning calls from OpenAI
, and other AI leaders to slow the pace of AI development, calling the push “self-serving.”
“Let’s all take a moment to understand how self-serving it is for OpenAI, Anthropic and other execs of big hyperscalers to talk of slowing things down,” Burry wrote on X.
He laid out four reasons for his skepticism:
1. LLMs are not AI and won't be AGI. There is nothing AI to slow down.
2. Competition is coming up fast, slowing benefits incumbents.
3. IPOs need hype & puffery; "we are so awesome it could become dangerous" is hype & puffery
4. Cover for real uncontrollable slowing growth as IPOs look to be pushed out

Burry said the push from OpenAI, Anthropic, and other major AI companies could benefit incumbents by slowing fast-moving competition. He also questioned the underlying premise, arguing that large language models are not artificial general intelligence and that there is therefore “nothing AI to slow down.”
He further suggested that talk of potentially dangerous AI could help sustain investor enthusiasm as companies prepare to go public.
OpenAI and Anthropic both submitted initial IPO filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission earlier this summer. However, OpenAI
CEO Sam Altman said that an IPO for his company won't come this year, as doing so would come at an "ill-advised moment."
Burry argued that the warnings could also provide “cover for real uncontrollable slowing growth as IPOs look to be pushed out.”

The comments come as several prominent AI leaders have called for a slower pace of development. In an essay on his personal website on Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said that the progress of improving AI model capabilities should be slowed down. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman responded to Amodei's essay on X. "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.
In his own X post, Elon Musk, founder of SpaceXAI (previously xAI), wrote, "Dario is right."

CEO Satya Nadella has also endorsed “the research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right as the design goal,” while Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis has previously backed a coordinated approach to slowing frontier AI development if risks mount. In July, he called for a U.S.-led global AI watchdog to screen the world's most advanced models.

title: Michael Burry calls AI leaders’ slowdown push ‘self-serving’
